text: Honestly, it wasn’t just some dramatic ending. The main worry was biological contamination: if Cassini’s orbit got messed up and it drifted into a moon like Enceladus or Titan, it could leave Earth microbes on worlds where we suspect water or even possible life. So the mission team chose to end the mission by diving into Saturn’s atmosphere. That was the so-called Grand Finale, and it kept the probe from accidentally crashing into a moon and possibly planting terrestrial organisms where we’re looking for native biology. It was the safest way to say goodbye.

That usually happens because the stationary leg is doing more than holding you up. Every time your pushing leg comes down, your standing leg has to absorb the jolt and keep your balance, and the muscles and joints in it get fatigued fast. It also has to resist twisting if your board moves or you're carving, so the knee and hip are working isometrically for a long time. If your stance is narrow or your weight is off-center, all that load lands on one side and can make the quad, hamstring or hip flexor ache. People usually blame the pushing leg or the board, but the stationary leg is the real stabilizer. If you're riding fast or on rough ground, the pain gets worse because every pothole sends a shock through the planted leg. What helps is not just rest; check your stance width, keep your knees slightly bent, and don't lock the knee. If the pain is in the front of the knee, it's often the quads overworking and not absorbing properly; if it's more in the hip or hamstring, it's likely a balance or posture issue. I'd also ask whether it's a dull ache after riding or a sharp pain during. Dull ache usually means fatigue or weak stabilizers. Sharp pain during riding is a warning that something in the knee, hip or ankle isn't handling the load. Strengthen the leg with squats, lunges, calf raises and single-leg stands, and warm up before you roll. Also, if you're always using the same pushing leg, your stationary leg becomes a fixed weak point. Try alternating push legs and keep your body centered. And honestly, a little discomfort from a hard day of skating isn't alarming, but a nagging pain that comes back the next day means you're asking that leg to do too much without enough strength or recovery.

You're touching on a really interesting point, and honestly it's a common misconception. When people use the term African American (or Afro-American, as you mentioned), they're generally referring to the ancestral roots of the community, not necessarily where the individuals were born or raised. The vast majority of Black Americans trace their lineage back to the transatlantic slave trade, where millions were forcibly brought from West and Central Africa. So the term isn't about current residence or immediate family origin, but rather a historical marker of that specific diaspora. I guess what gets confusing is that people assume the term means someone whose immediate family is currently living in Africa, but that's not quite how it works. Of course, not every Black American is of purely African descent, and there's a lot of mixed heritage and diverse backgrounds within the community. But the label is primarily a nod to that historical connection to the African continent. I think it's less about geography and more about that deep historical and cultural lineage. Plus, the African American designation was actually popularized in the 1960s as a way to assert a distinct, proud identity, moving away from older terms. So it's a conscious cultural choice rooted in that ancestral connection, making the label much broader than just a simple geographic origin.

Yeah, I get the appeal of that idea, but I think you're underestimating what "adverse effects" actually means. A drug that makes you feel amazing without any direct damage sounds like a dream, but once you start thinking about how the brain reacts, it gets way more complicated than just "pleasure without side effects."

The big problem is tolerance. Your body figures out how to handle the drug, so over time you need more of it to get the same high. And that's not just a physical thing; it's psychological too. Once your brain is wired to expect the drug, the compulsion to keep taking it becomes part of the picture, whether you notice it as a problem or not. So even a drug with no chemical toxicity could still produce that "I need more" cycle.

Then there's withdrawal, which is basically the other side of tolerance. If you stop, the brain's reward system is messed up and you get that low. That's not just "feeling bad" for a moment; it's a real physiological state. So if a drug had literally zero adverse effects, would it still produce tolerance and withdrawal? If yes, then it's still not the perfect pleasure pill you're imagining. If no, then it probably wouldn't be as intense or addictive, which is exactly the point.

I mean, I can see why you'd want something that hits hard and leaves no mark, but the body doesn't really do "no mark." Even caffeine, which a lot of us treat like it's just tea, can be a mild drug. We get used to it, and if you stop, you get that headache and fatigue. So the idea of zero adverse effects is a pretty high bar. What you're really asking for is a drug that doesn't train your brain to want it, and I don't think we have that.

As far as I know, the pleasure and the tolerance are linked in a way that makes this trade-off basically unavoidable. You can't get the intense euphoria of something like heroin or cocaine without the brain's reward system adapting to it, which is where the compulsive use starts. I guess that's the core of why people talk about drugs being "bad" even when the drug itself isn't doing chemical damage. It's not just the side effects you can measure in a lab; it's also the way your brain gets hooked on the expectation of the high.

Hi there,
That sounds like your brain was still in the silk task when you answered. Repeating a word and spelling it loads working memory, and then the cow question landed right on top of that. Milk is the word that sits next to cow in our mental dictionary, so when attention slipped, the strong association fired instead of the careful one. It’s not that you forgot what cows drink; it’s more that the repeated task made automatic associations take over. You probably didn't make the mistake on purpose, and your mind just grabbed the most obvious word attached to cows. If it happens often, you might be tired or distracted, but a one-off slip is pretty normal. No need to worry about it. I wouldn't read too much into it; it’s just your mind taking the easy route. Especially after that repetition exercise, your attention wasn't fully on the new question.
Best,
Your friend

Hey Sam,

Good question. Honestly, I think the main difference is that a 3-in-1 product has to do too much at once. It's basically a compromise. It's meant to clean hair, condition hair, and wash the body, and because it's trying to be all of those things, it's never really optimized for any single job. I mean, a dedicated shampoo has surfactants chosen for hair cleaning, a conditioner focuses on detangling and softening, and a body wash is formulated for skin. When you mix all those needs into one bottle, you get something that's okay-ish across the board but not especially good at any one task.

A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is similar, but at least it's focused on hair, so it's a bit more specialized than the 3-in-1. That said, even that can leave hair feeling greasy or under-cleaned, depending on the formula. As far as I know, the real trade-off is convenience versus performance. The all-in-one works fine for a quick wash or when you're traveling and want one bottle for everything, but if you care about your hair or skin, dedicated products usually do their own job better.

Anyway, glad you asked. I was curious about this too.

Best,
Alex

Yeah, that one's harder than it looks. The direct way is GPS: they put receivers on stable points on a continent and compare positions repeatedly over months or years. That turns centimeters per year into a speed, which matches plate motion pretty well. They also use satellite laser ranging and similar geodetic methods for more precise tracking.

For the longer story, geologists look at fossils, rock types, and the fit of ancient coastlines. Seafloor patterns and magnetic stripes show plates spreading at roughly steady speeds, and old mineral magnetization can tell where plates used to be. The GPS numbers and the geological record should line up, and they mostly do, so you get both a current speed and a historical check. If you mean how fast a continent moves relative to another, that's just comparing two GPS sites on different plates over time. Different plates move at different speeds, usually a few centimeters per year. You don't need to see it with your eyes; the instruments make the tiny changes visible. I'd say the instruments are doing most of the seeing. It's one of those cases where you're trusting the measurement chain, and the geology checking it.

Hope that clears it up.

Cheers,
Me

Honestly, I think the key point is not that inbreeding directly lowers IQ. It makes harmful recessive genes more likely to show up. In a population, genes that affect cognitive ability are often rare and recessive, meaning one copy usually hides in the background. When parents are closely related, they share more DNA, so a child can inherit the same variant from both sides. As far as I know, that increased chance of two matching copies is what researchers mean by inbreeding depression. I mean, two cousins carry a few more shared mutations than strangers do, and some of those can affect brain development. The closer the relatives, the more of these rare variants are likely to land together. That's why family history can matter. So you can think of it as a shift in risk.

When an injury happens in the arm, it often seems less painful than an injury to the torso, head, or leg, but that is not because the arm is numb. A lot of it is how your brain reads the injury. A wound in the arm is usually far from major organs, so it feels less threatening and lowers the body's alarm response. The arm has muscle and soft tissue that can absorb a hit, but it also has nerves, so a cut, punch, or bullet can still be quite painful. In the chest or abdomen, even a small injury can involve organs, so the reaction is stronger. You also matter: if you know an arm injury is much less likely to be dangerous, you may tense up less and the pain seems smaller. That is why an arm wound can feel manageable even when the tissue is clearly damaged.

I know this one trips people up, and I think the confusing bit is that both are colorless gases, but they hit your body in very different ways. I mean, carbon dioxide isn't harmless in every sense: if it builds up in a sealed room, it can make you drowsy or short of breath because it displaces oxygen. But at normal outdoor levels it's just part of the air we breathe. Carbon monoxide is a different kind of problem. I think of it less as a gas that chokes you and more as something that quietly takes over the oxygen-delivery system in your blood.

The key difference is this: your red blood cells carry oxygen with a protein called hemoglobin. Carbon monoxide sticks to hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, around 200 times stronger by some estimates. So when you breathe CO in, it doesn't just add another gas to the mix. It occupies the same binding sites oxygen would use, which means your blood has less capacity to carry oxygen. That's why CO poisoning can be so dangerous even at low, almost imperceptible levels: you don't get a strong warning smell, and the first signs can be headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion, and then things can worsen.

For a new colleague, I'd keep it practical. CO is common around poorly ventilated combustion sources, like a car in a garage or a faulty boiler, and it's more dangerous where people can't open a window quickly. CO2 is something we already live with; your lungs are built to handle normal amounts, although in crowded or sealed spaces it can become a problem. The real danger with CO isn't that CO2 is the other one and CO is the bad one in an absolute sense. It's that CO interferes directly with oxygen transport, while CO2 mainly becomes an issue when it accumulates enough to lower oxygen.

When the crew calls brace, you sit or lie down, bend forward, and keep your head low and hands protected. The point is to put your body into a compact shape that lets your own muscles and the seat absorb impact rather than letting your head, chest, or legs take the full hit. In a crash or hard landing, inertia keeps moving you forward. Leaning forward and keeping the airway open helps reduce sudden strain on the neck and back, and keeps you from being thrown against the seat or cabin structures. It will not make the crash painless, but it can reduce the chance of serious injury by controlling how your body reacts to the impact.

As a new colleague, you needn't remember the wording of the call, but you should know what to do. If seated, stay in your seat, bend your knees, hold onto something safe, and keep your head away from hard surfaces. The posture may feel strange, but in a severe event it is one of the simple steps that can make the difference between a survivable impact and a much worse one. Think of it as helping your body work with the crash, not against it.

I think most of it is a difference in what well-known means now. Before the industrial era, businesses were usually local workshops, trading posts, or guild shops, and they rarely tried to be famous far beyond their home market. I mean, they had clients and regulars, not brands with mass advertising. Some old trading houses did cross borders, but their names didn't stick in public memory the way modern firms do. Add poor records, ownership changes, and standardized manufacturing, and it's hard for a pre-industrial company to still be recognizable today. It's more that brand recognition only became possible later.

I keep running into the same confusion: why would a bank loan be cheaper when the dealership advertises lower rates? I think the headline rate is the part dealerships know will get your attention, while the actual cost hides in the fine print. A 1.9% or 0% dealer promo can look unbeatable, but if that promo comes with a financing fee, a higher purchase price, or mandatory add-ons, the total can be higher than a bank at a somewhat higher rate.

Take a car with a negotiated price of $20,000 financed over 60 months. A bank at 6.5% on that amount comes to about $23,400 in total payments. If a dealer offers 0% but the car price is pushed to $23,000 and a $1,500 financing fee is added, the all-in cost is about $24,500. The lower rate on the loan is not the same as the lower total cost of the purchase. Dealers can make up for the cheap money by raising the sticker price, requiring a service plan, or adding a document fee, so the car itself costs more even if the financing looks free.

What I have learned is to compare the loan amount, monthly payment, and total amount repaid, not just the interest rate. A dealer quote might say 1.9%, but if the vehicle price was pushed from $20,000 to $21,500, that extra $1,500 is real money. The bank may charge a higher rate, yet because the purchase price stayed where you negotiated it, the all-in cost can come out lower. There are also pre-pay fees, insurance bundling, and payment terms that can flip which option is truly cheaper. A bank's loan statement gives you the exact number you will pay at the end. The dealer's package may look friendlier month to month, but the sticker price and fees are where the deal can quietly drift upward. If you only look at the rate, you are comparing apples and oranges.

My position is simple: the dealership's lower rate is often a sales tool, and the bank can be cheaper when you strip out the dealer add-ons and compare the full cost of the deal. Do not let the rate alone decide it. Look at the vehicle price, the fees, and the total of every payment, and you will usually see why the bank can win. That is how I stopped getting tricked by a low interest rate on the financing line while the car price quietly rose.

I keep getting tripped up by the patchwork of marijuana laws across US states. One state might treat it as a legal adult-use market, while its neighbor still calls it a medical necessity or treats possession like a misdemeanor. That’s not just annoying; it means a person can drive across a border and the plant in their bag changes legal character. My position is that states should set their own rules, because local governments know what residents need and how to tax and regulate the market. I think federal law should stop overruling state decisions, but I don’t want states to use legality as an excuse to skip age limits, retail licensing, testing, and clear penalties for driving under the influence. Legalization only helps if it comes with sensible guardrails. I’m not a lawyer, but after following this for years, my gut says the current mess hurts ordinary people most.

I always found the idea of body electricity a little funny. I mean, we don't have tiny batteries in our nerves. What happens is simpler and stranger: sodium and potassium ions moving across cell membranes. When a signal travels down a nerve, sodium floods in and potassium floods out, and that charge shift is the electrical event. My position is that this isn't some secret current we generate; it's chemistry pushing charged atoms through channels in the membrane. I find that more beautiful than 'the body makes lightning'. Honestly, it's really just a tiny voltage shift, not even a spark.

I still think the best samples come from actually sitting with the record, not just searching a database for a hit. When I was working on a track a few years ago, I spent an evening flipping through vinyl I’d picked up secondhand, and what pulled me in was a few seconds of a forgotten instrumental break, not the chorus everyone already knows. That’s the kind of thing you only find by listening for a while, letting your ear drift. You hear the room tone, the tape hiss, the way a horn section sits slightly behind the beat, and that’s the texture you want. A database might give you the famous 10 seconds; the record gives you the other five.

The practical side is where it gets unglamorous. If I wanted to use that snippet in a release, I’d need to clear the master and the publishing, which means finding the people who own the recording and the song separately. Sometimes that’s a label, sometimes an estate, sometimes a small production company nobody’s heard of. The clearance process can take weeks and the fee can surprise you, so I usually budget a little extra and ask early. I don’t want to be in the position of releasing a track and then getting a letter.

Once the sample is cleared, the actual music-making starts. You chop the snippet into pieces, loop the part that has the rhythmic identity, pitch it to key, maybe time-stretch it if the old record runs a little slow. The old recording quality is part of the character; I wouldn’t clean it up until the feel is right. A bit of the original crackle and room sound can make the sample feel alive rather than polished.

One thing I’d tell a younger producer is to write down exactly where the sample came from: artist, song, side, timestamp, and who owns it. That small habit saves headaches later. I once assumed a track was free to use because it was obscure, and only found out later that a rights holder was still active. So I keep a simple note for every source, and I ask before I commit.

I’m not against using libraries of cleared material, and sometimes they’re the fast route. But I still prefer the hunt. The question of how musicians sample older songs isn’t just a technical question; it’s also about what you’re willing to spend time listening for and the patience to get the rights straight. That’s where the music actually becomes yours to use.

I’ve spent enough time white-knuckling headaches to know it isn’t really my brain deciding to hurt. I’m convinced most headaches feel bad because of the stuff around the brain, not the brain’s grey matter itself. For me it’s the tension: when I’m stressed or haven’t slept, my jaw and neck tighten, and that tension radiates into my temples. I’ve also noticed the classic pattern: a day with too much screen, too little water, and a skipped meal turns into a dull pressure that gets worse if I push through it. I don’t know every mechanism, but my take is that the pain comes from irritated blood vessels, overactive nerves, and inflamed membranes, not from the brain “thinking” in pain. That’s why resting in a dark room, hydrating, and easing the neck tension often takes the edge off, and sometimes even a good night’s sleep helps, while ignoring it can make the cycle worse.

I can't tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We put our names on their totally useless digital waitlist, then were told to come back at 8:23 p.m. to pay. I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. It came to about $130 for two, which felt pretty steep. I had figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed there was no steak. At that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us, so I just ate the crab legs. The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

To be honest, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

Keeping it

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, and it’s always when I’m typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. I asked the seller what they were, and the answer took a week. By then I had pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version, so I’ve sat through lots of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly it was mixed, maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too; the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, just if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity. Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once, too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, more must be better, so they crammed everything in. Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. A few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. The shirts never arrived because the sales representative recorded the delivery address incorrectly. Her handwritten “7” was interpreted as a “1,” so the package went to 5401 instead of 5407. The residents at 5401 brought it to the local UPS store for return, and it was never seen or heard from again. I guess we didn't learn about it until several weeks later. During the dispute, we placed an additional order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner handled it at that stage. I mean, he acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly responsible because we had not been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company and eventually received a credit.
